title: Contemporary evolution of insect thermal sensitivity across exposure durations and ontogeny
content:
Abstract
The responses of ectotherm growth and developmental rates to temperature depend on the duration of exposure and development stage. These rates determine fitness responses to climate change and variability and are subject to selection, potentially leading to evolutionary change. We repeat a study of thermal sensitivity of larval growth rates in a population of the cabbage white butterfly (Pieris rapae) to assess evolutionary responses to 25 years (more than 75 generations) of climate change. Modern caterpillars grow faster, particularly at warm temperatures that have become more prevalent in recent decades. Growth rate increases are most pronounced at shorter exposure durations and earlier in larval development. Our study points to the potential for contemporary evolution consistent with a response to recent climate change in a widespread and dispersive species.
